cases.user_message: Готовлю материал про застройщика. В марте 2024 у них на сайте была страница /news/zhk-severny с пресс-релизом, где был указан срок сдачи «IV квартал 2025». Сейчас там написано «II квартал 2027», и дата публикации на странице осталась старая, никакой пометки об изменении нет. Мне нужно показать редактору, когда именно текст поменяли, и приложить доказательства. Я знаю, что есть архив интернета, но там по этой странице сотни снимков, листать их руками нереально. Как это сделать быстро и так, чтобы результат нельзя было оспорить? Питон знаю на базовом уровне.
cases.why_in_scope: The skill tells the model to use the CDX API with collapse=digest so that only captures with changed content remain (same digest = identical content), narrow by from/to dates, fetch the two bounding captures in raw id_ mode to diff clean HTML without the archive toolbar, keep to about 1 request per second, and cite the Wayback captures with their timestamps. A strong model without it tends to suggest paging through the calendar UI or downloading every snapshot and diffing them all, missing the digest-based dedup and the raw mode, which is exactly what makes this fast and clean.
rubric: Recommends querying the Wayback Machine CDX API for the page URL and deduplicating captures by content digest (collapse=digest or comparing the digest field), explaining that an unchanged digest means unchanged content, so only the few distinct versions need inspection.

Explains retrieving the original page HTML without the Wayback toolbar/injected markup (the id_ suffix after the timestamp) before diffing, or otherwise addresses archive-injected noise in the comparison.

Gives a concrete way to bound the change: the last capture with the old wording and the first capture with the new wording, cited by their archive URLs/timestamps as evidence, with the caveat that the edit happened somewhere between those two captures, not at an exact moment.

Stays practical for a basic Python user (concrete steps or a short script) and mentions pacing requests to the archive (e.g. about one per second, with a pause/backoff on errors) rather than hammering it.

cases.user_message: I'm trying to reconstruct how a competitor's pricing page (acme-analytics.io/pricing) changed over the last 3 years using archive.org. I wrote a Python loop that hits web.archive.org/web/<timestamp>/acme-analytics.io/pricing for every timestamp I got from the CDX endpoint and parses the plan names and prices with BeautifulSoup. Three problems: (1) there are ~1,400 captures; I tried skipping duplicates by md5-hashing the HTML I download, but almost every hash comes out different even when the page looks the same, so I still fetch everything and the run takes hours; (2) my selectors sometimes grab junk that isn't from their site at all, and some links in the HTML point to web.archive.org instead of their domain; (3) after a few hundred requests I start getting errors and connection resets. How should I restructure this?
cases.why_in_scope: The skill supplies the specific fixes: dedup server-side with collapse=digest (plus statuscode:200 / mimetype:text/html filters) using the archive's own content digest instead of hashing downloaded pages; the id_ raw mode after the timestamp to get the original HTML without the Wayback toolbar and rewritten links (which is also why the user's own hashes all differ); and about 1 request/second with backoff. A strong model without it may suggest normalising the HTML before hashing or stripping the toolbar with custom parsing, which still downloads all 1,400 captures.
rubric: Recommends deduplicating before any download using the CDX digest (collapse=digest, or skipping rows whose digest field repeats), noting that identical digest means identical archived content, so only distinct versions are fetched.

Identifies that the junk, the web.archive.org links and the differing hashes come from the Wayback toolbar/URL rewriting injected into replayed pages, and recommends fetching raw captures by adding id_ after the timestamp (e.g. web.archive.org/web/<timestamp>id_/acme-analytics.io/pricing).
Addresses the errors/resets by slowing down (on the order of one request per second or slower) with retry and backoff, framed as respecting the archive's rate limits.
Gives a coherent restructured pipeline (filtered CDX query -> fetch distinct raw captures -> parse -> dated change timeline) that fits the user's Python/BeautifulSoup setup.

checker_notes: Case 2 made subtler: the user now already tried hashing downloaded HTML and got all-different hashes (toolbar noise), so the answer must reach server-side digest dedup plus id_ raw mode rather than generic post-download hashing; tightened rubric item 1 so status/mime filtering alone does not pass and loosened the exact 1 req/s figure. Case 1 kept; its throttling item now accepts any pacing with backoff instead of a script-format requirement.
